name: The Salvation Army USA: services in the US (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the Salvation Army's services in the US (its overseas work has its own model).
summary: The Salvation Army is a church that runs the largest network of social services in the United States: food (184 million meals), shelters (10 million nights), help with bills, holiday gifts, housing placements, residential addiction recovery funded by its thrift stores, and community centres. Our model of every US programme in fiscal 2025 (October 2024 to September 2025), with the thrift stores' running costs, clients' day-care fees and the overseas work (a model of its own) left out, values the food, goods, bills and services at what families would otherwise pay on the site's log-income scale, shelter by a room's value and the deaths it averts, housing placements by the trials' extra years housed, recovery by remissions and deaths, and the community and church programmes by life satisfaction. It comes to about 0.003 years of healthy life per $1,000, about a thousandth of the site's global-health median, because the help is small next to what even poor US households consume: about $30 of food, goods, money and services a person in a year against consumption of about $18,000, a 0.2% gain on the log scale, where a GiveDirectly transfer raises a Kenyan household's consumption by about 40%. About half the result comes from food, goods, money and services, a quarter from shelter. Every branch is discounted for missing data, since none of the Salvation Army's services has a controlled evaluation: food, goods and money, shelter, placements, recovery, community programmes and worship. The biggest uncertainties are what families would have got without the Salvation Army, how well its counts reflect help delivered, and how much the recovery programme changes.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: US programme spending in fiscal 2025, net of the thrift stores' running costs and day-care fees
rows.explainer: All four programme lines of the combined US accounts (corps community centres, rehabilitation, residential and institutional services, other social services), less what the Adult Rehabilitation Centers' thrift stores cost to run and less the day-care fees clients paid (their own money for a service valued below net of them), and less the overseas work paid through these accounts (the World Service Office and the territories' support for the international Salvation Army), which is modelled separately (salvation-army-charityevals-international) and weighted by its spending on the charity's page. The stores are a self-financing trading arm: their sales pay for their own staff, trucks and rent, and only their net contribution pays for the recovery programme. Counting their gross running costs as charitable spending would make every donated dollar look as if it bought less help than it does. Fiscal year 1 October 2024 to 30 September 2025, the latest with audited accounts and service statistics for the same period.

rows.label: Total expenses, fiscal 2025 (all programmes, management, fundraising)
rows.explainer: The shared Salvation Army figure (facts/salvation_army.json), read by this model and by the overseas model so the two split the combined accounts in full. The national combined statement adds up the audited statements of the six US corporations (National Headquarters, the World Service Office and the four territories), intercorporate transactions eliminated. The combination itself is unaudited; each part is audited. Dollars in thousands in the report.

rows.label: Programme expenses, fiscal 2025 (all four programme lines)
rows.explainer: The shared Salvation Army figure (facts/salvation_army.json), read by this model and by the overseas model so the two split the combined accounts in full. Corps community centres $893.5M, rehabilitation $739.6M, residential and institutional services $552.9M and other social services $1,360.3M (p. 23). These include donated food, toys and clothing at their fair value, which is right here: the goods are part of the help, and a donor's dollar buys a share of the whole bundle.

rows.label: Rehabilitation programme expenses, fiscal 2025 (Adult Rehabilitation Centers and their thrift stores)
rows.explainer: The shared Salvation Army figure (facts/salvation_army.json), read by this model and by the overseas model so the two split the combined accounts in full. The Adult Rehabilitation Centers' whole cost: the residential recovery programme and the thrift stores that fund it (the Western Territory's audited functional-expense statement shows the line is mostly salaries and occupancy, with almost no direct assistance, which is the stores' profile).

rows.label: Share of rehabilitation expenses that is the recovery programme itself (not the stores)
rows.explainer: The shared Salvation Army figure (facts/salvation_army.json), read by this model and by the overseas model so the two split the combined accounts in full. No published split, so a judgment from three cross-checks. (1) Sales to the public were $553.2M in fiscal 2025 (p. 23); if store sales roughly cover the stores' own costs, the rest of the rehabilitation line, $186M or 25%, is the programme. (2) Beds × cost: the Eastern Territory runs 26 centres with 2,049 beds (saconnects.org, January 2026), so about 108 rehabilitation centres nationally hold roughly 8,500 beds; at $40-80 a bed-day for a work-therapy residence that is $125-250M, 17-34% of the line. (3) The one territory with public audited accounts, the Western, had sales to the public of $131.4M against a rehabilitation line of $150.1M in fiscal 2023 (statements pp. 5-6), which by the logic of (1) leaves 12.5%. Range 10-40%.

rows.label: Programme service fees paid by clients, fiscal 2025
rows.explainer: The shared Salvation Army figure (facts/salvation_army.json), read by this model and by the overseas model so the two split the combined accounts in full. Fees clients pay for services (sliding-fee day care, camps, Kroc centre memberships, rent in residences).

rows.label: Share of programme fees that are day-care fees
rows.explainer: The shared Salvation Army figure (facts/salvation_army.json), read by this model and by the overseas model so the two split the combined accounts in full. No split is published. 67 day care centres with 17,617 participants at sliding fees of a few thousand dollars a year would collect $20-80M of the $167M; camps, Kroc memberships and residents' rent the rest. 30% (15-50%).

rows.label: Day-care fees, netted out of the cost
rows.explainer: Day care is valued net of what families pay, so its fees come out of the cost. The other fees stay in: camps, memberships and residents' rent buy outcomes valued gross here (community wellbeing, shelter), so cost and value are both gross.

rows.label: Overseas work paid through the US accounts (modelled separately)
rows.explainer: The World Service Office's programmes (fiscal 2025, by sector) and the US territories' world-services money to International Headquarters (the Self-Denial Fund, headquarters support and restricted gifts, mostly to the Officers' Support Endowment Fund, from the International Trust's accounts, pounds at the 2024 rate: the Trust's year to March 2025 is mostly 2024). It is spent abroad on other kinds of work, so it has a model of its own (salvation-army-charityevals-international), weighted by this spending on the charity's page; it is left out of this model's cost and outcomes.

rows.label: Thrift stores' own running costs (left out of programme spending)
rows.explainer: The rehabilitation line less the recovery programme. Corps-run thrift stores (in the corps line) are small next to the ARC stores and are left in.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ program expenses)
rows.explainer: Management and fundraising spread over the programmes in proportion to their cost, as GiveWell and ACE do, with the thrift stores' running costs and day-care fees out of both totals (they are paid by the stores' sales and by the clients, not by donors).

rows.label: Cost of the modelled program, including overhead
Basic social services given in fiscal 2025 (food, clothing, financial help): the food, goods and money branch

source.title: The Salvation Army USA, 2026 National Annual Report: Financial Summary & Statistical Highlights (fiscal year ended 30 September 2025)

rows.explainer: The report's count of basic social services, the closest it has to households helped with food, goods and bills. It counts touchpoints, so a family helped twice may be counted twice. That hardly matters here: the value below is the total value handed out (meals, items, bills paid) spread over these households, and on the log scale a small gift's value is almost proportional to its size, so splitting it over more or fewer people barely changes the result.

rows.label: People per household
rows.explainer: The site's US household size (@household_size.united_states): food parcels, bills paid and holiday help serve the whole household.

rows.label: People reached by food, goods and money help
Cost per person reached (context: the whole charity's cost over the main branch's people)
rows.explainer: Context: compare with the charity's own figure and with other models of the family.

rows.label: Meals provided, fiscal 2025

source.title: The Salvation Army USA, 2026 National Annual Report: Financial Summary & Statistical Highlights (fiscal year ended 30 September 2025)

rows.explainer: Hot meals, food-pantry food counted as meals, and meals in shelters, camps and disaster canteens. Some of these meals are also part of the shelter and rehabilitation stays below; their food is counted here only, and the shelter's value is the bed alone.

rows.label: USDA Thrifty Food Plan, monthly cost for a family of four (June 2025 prices, fiscal 2026 SNAP)

source.title: No Kid Hungry, The Thrifty Food Plan (FY 2026), summarising USDA FNS's June 2025 cost
source.quote: In FY 2026, The TFP estimates that a typical family of four would need to spend about $994 a month for a balanced and cost-conscious diet.

rows.explainer: The cheapest nutritious grocery basket, what a poor family would otherwise buy for the food a pantry or a meal programme gives (groceries, not restaurant meals). Range: low, about $2.60 a meal (Feeding America's cheapest county, Map the Meal Gap 2025); high, nearer USDA's Low-Cost plan, for hot meals and shelter meals that cost more to make than groceries.

rows.label: Meals per person per month
rows.explainer: Three meals a day over the average month: the conversion Map the Meal Gap uses (weekly food spending over 21 meals).

rows.label: Meals per person per day

source.title: Feeding America, How We Got the Map Data (Map the Meal Gap)
source.quote: The average dollar amount spent on food per week by food-secure individuals is divided by 21

rows.explainer: 21 meals a week, three a day: the meal definition behind food banks' meal counts.

rows.label: People in the Thrifty Food Plan's reference family

source.title: No Kid Hungry, The Thrifty Food Plan (FY 2026)
source.quote: the USDA estimates the cost of those groceries at four different budget levels

rows.explainer: The reference family of four (two adults aged 20-50, two children aged 6-11) the plan is priced for.

rows.label: Grocery cost of a meal at the Thrifty Food Plan (US$)
rows.explainer: About $2.72: the plan's monthly cost per person over 91 meals. Groceries, since a pantry's food replaces groceries a poor family would buy; Map the Meal Gap's $3.58 is all food spending of food-secure people, restaurants included.

rows.label: Tangible items distributed (clothing, furniture, gifts), fiscal 2025

source.title: The Salvation Army USA, 2026 National Annual Report: Financial Summary & Statistical Highlights (fiscal year ended 30 September 2025)

rows.explainer: Clothing, furniture, school supplies and holiday gifts (Angel Tree), including the items handed out after disasters. The report's 2,562,029 holiday-assistance touchpoints are these gifts and holiday meals, already in the item and meal counts, so they get no value of their own.

rows.label: Value of an item handed out (US$)
rows.explainer: Mostly donated clothing and toys: a judgment anchored on thrift-store prices for used clothing ($4-10), new toys under Angel Tree ($15-30 a gift) and furniture at the top. No published average.

rows.label: Households given financial assistance (rent, utilities, medical, transport), fiscal 2025

source.title: The Salvation Army USA, 2026 National Annual Report: Financial Summary & Statistical Highlights (fiscal year ended 30 September 2025)
source.quote: Households Provided With Financial Assistance (Housing, Medical, Utilities, Transportation, Misc) 1,386,097

rows.explainer: Bills paid on a household's behalf: as good as cash to the household, so not discounted as in-kind help. Transport help (729,344 bus passes and fuel cards, a separate line on p. 21) is part of this financial assistance by the report's own definition and its cash is in the audited direct assistance below, so it gets no value of its own.

rows.label: Western Territory: direct assistance, fiscal 2023

source.title: The Salvation Army USA, Western Territory and Affiliates, Combined Financial Statements, 2023 and 2022 (audited)
source.page: p. 7, Combined Statements of Functional Expenses

rows.explainer: Everything handed to clients, in kind or in money, in the one territory with public audited accounts.

rows.label: Western Territory: donated food, clothing, Christmas gifts and household goods, and government food, fiscal 2023

source.title: The Salvation Army USA, Western Territory and Affiliates, Combined Financial Statements, 2023 and 2022 (audited)
source.quote: Food from public support 109,313; Clothing 23,933; Angel Tree and other Christmas gifts 16,006; Household goods 17,112 ... Food from government agencies 5,735

rows.explainer: The goods the note says are recorded mainly in direct assistance, government food commodities included (the 'other' line, $12.2M, mostly vehicles sold, is left out). What is left of direct assistance is roughly the cash paid out for bills.

rows.label: Western Territory's share of the households given financial assistance
rows.explainer: The Western Territory spent $870.6M of the country's programme expenses in fiscal 2023, about a quarter of the national total ($3.44B in fiscal 2024, p. 23); its share of households is taken as about the same, 24% (18-30%).

rows.label: Financial help per household (US$)
rows.explainer: Cash direct assistance in the Western Territory's audited accounts (direct assistance less the donated and government goods recorded in it, about $24M) over its share of the households helped, put from fiscal-2023 into 2025 prices by the US consumer price index (Convention 8): about $76 a household, the national figure taken at the Western rate. Bills paid on a household's behalf count at full value.

rows.label: Veterans services given, fiscal 2025

source.title: The Salvation Army USA, 2026 National Annual Report: Financial Summary & Statistical Highlights (fiscal year ended 30 September 2025)

rows.explainer: Mostly Supportive Services for Veteran Families (44 programmes): case management and temporary financial help to keep or regain housing; their housing placements are in the placements count.

rows.label: Temporary financial help and services per veteran household (US$)
rows.explainer: SSVF pays rent arrears, deposits and utilities for a few months besides case management, much more per household than one-off emergency help, but many of the touchpoints are case management only. $500 (100-2,000).

rows.label: Pathway of Hope families, fiscal 2025

source.title: The Salvation Army USA, 2026 National Annual Report: Financial Summary & Statistical Highlights (fiscal year ended 30 September 2025)

rows.explainer: Families in the Salvation Army's case-management programme towards steady income and housing.

rows.label: Income gain per Pathway of Hope family in the year (US$)
rows.explainer: No outcome evaluation is published. Anchor: case management for low-income families towards self-sufficiency, such as HUD's Family Self-Sufficiency programme, showed no significant earnings gain after three years in MDRC's randomised evaluation (2021), with a few hundred dollars at the point estimate; $200 (0-1,500).

rows.label: People given employment assistance, fiscal 2025

source.title: The Salvation Army USA, 2026 National Annual Report: Financial Summary & Statistical Highlights (fiscal year ended 30 September 2025)

rows.explainer: Job search help, training and placement.

rows.label: Extra earnings in the first year per person given employment help (US$)
rows.explainer: Light-touch job-search assistance in US randomised evaluations (job clubs, reemployment services) raises earnings by a few hundred to about $1,500 in the first year; most of the Salvation Army's help is lighter (referrals, job-readiness classes). $500 (0-1,500).

rows.label: Years until people given job-search help and others earn the same (fade-out)
rows.explainer: In the same evaluations the gain fades within two or three years, as the control group finds work too: 2 years (1-3).

rows.label: Extra earnings per person given employment help, discounted over the gain's years (US$)
rows.explainer: The first year's gain over the years it lasts, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Medical care given, fiscal 2025

source.title: The Salvation Army USA, 2026 National Annual Report: Financial Summary & Statistical Highlights (fiscal year ended 30 September 2025)

rows.explainer: Visits at the 11 medical clinics.

rows.label: Value of a clinic visit to the patient (US$)
rows.explainer: A primary-care visit's price for an uninsured patient ($100-300), more with medicines; judgment $200 (50-600), counted as in-kind help.

rows.label: Anti-human-trafficking services given, fiscal 2025

source.title: The Salvation Army USA, 2026 National Annual Report: Financial Summary & Statistical Highlights (fiscal year ended 30 September 2025)

rows.explainer: Case management, safe housing and legal referral for survivors (24 programmes).

rows.label: Value of anti-trafficking services per survivor (US$)
rows.explainer: Weeks of case management and some nights of safe housing at their cost to buy ($1,000-3,000), a referral only at the low end; judgment $1,500 (300-6,000), counted as in-kind help. Their wellbeing gain beyond that value is not counted.

rows.label: Correctional services given, fiscal 2025

source.title: The Salvation Army USA, 2026 National Annual Report: Financial Summary & Statistical Highlights (fiscal year ended 30 September 2025)

rows.explainer: Prison ministry, probation supervision services and help on release.

rows.label: Value of correctional services per person (US$)
rows.explainer: Mostly visits and re-entry help; some court-ordered probation supervision the person would otherwise pay a private provider for ($30-60 a month). Judgment $100 (20-500), counted as in-kind help.

rows.label: Emergency disaster assistance given, fiscal 2025

source.title: The Salvation Army USA, 2026 National Annual Report: Financial Summary & Statistical Highlights (fiscal year ended 30 September 2025)

rows.explainer: People helped at 972 disasters. Their meals and items are already in the meal and item counts; this row is only what else they got.

rows.label: Disaster help per person beyond meals and items (US$)
rows.explainer: Gift cards, cleanup and hygiene supplies not counted as items, hydration and emotional and spiritual care; judgment $50 (10-200).

rows.label: Day care participants, fiscal 2025

source.title: The Salvation Army USA, 2026 National Annual Report: Financial Summary & Statistical Highlights (fiscal year ended 30 September 2025)

rows.explainer: Children (and some adults) in 67 Salvation Army day care centres; counted once a year.

rows.label: Value of a year's day care place to the family, net of fees (US$)
rows.explainer: Centre-based child care costs US families about $10,000-15,000 a year at market prices; the Salvation Army charges sliding fees (netted out of the cost with all programme fees) and many places are part-year or part-day, so the value net of fees per participant is a judgment of $4,000 ($1,000-10,000).

rows.label: What in-kind goods are worth to the family, as a share of their retail price
rows.explainer: Food, clothing and care given in kind are worth less to the family than the same money, since they can't choose what to buy; households who would have bought the goods anyway value them at about full price. 80% (60-100%), anchored on the literature valuing in-kind transfers (food stamps at 80-95% of face value for most households, less for goods the family wouldn't have bought). Bills paid count at full value.

rows.label: Value received per person in the year (US$, food, goods, money and services)
rows.explainer: All food, goods, bills paid, transport, day care, clinic visits, anti-trafficking, correctional and disaster services handed out, and the earnings that case management and job help add, at what the family would otherwise pay (in-kind goods at their cash-equivalent share), over the people reached. Only money value: the relief food brings is counted here once, not again as wellbeing.
rows.formula: ((meals_provided * meal_value + tangible_items * item_value + day_care_children * day_care_value + medical_visits * medical_visit_value + trafficking_survivors * trafficking_service_value + correctional_served * correctional_value + disaster_assisted * disaster_extra_value) * inkind_cash_equivalence + financial_assistance_households * assistance_per_household + veterans_served * veterans_help_value + pathway_of_hope_families * pathway_income_gain + employment_assisted * employment_earnings_gain) / people_reached

rows.label: Average consumption per person in the US, in fiscal-2025 dollars (US$)
rows.explainer: The site's US figure (@united_states.consumption_per_person_2024, World Bank, 2024 dollars) put into 2025 prices by the US consumer price index (@cpi.usa_2025 / @cpi.usa_2024, about +2.6%, Convention 8), so it is in the same year's dollars as the help valued against it (fiscal 2025, October 2024 to September 2025).

rows.label: The people served's consumption per person, as a share of the average
rows.explainer: People who come to a food pantry or for help with a bill are mostly below or near the poverty line. The anchor is the poorest fifth of US households, who spend 45% of the average per household (@united_states.ce_lowest_quintile_vs_all_2024), and more per person since their households are smaller; Salvation Army clients are poorer than the bottom fifth on average (eligibility for most help is at or below 130-200% of the poverty line, about 25-35% of mean consumption per person). Judgment 30% (20-50%).

rows.label: The people served's consumption per person (US$)
Years the help keeps its money value for the people served
rows.explainer: A year's food, goods and bills are consumed within the year: one year, the flow against one year's cost (Convention 3).

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person, discounted
rows.explainer: The site's one log-income scale at the clients' own consumption: a dollar does far less for a US household than for one living on a few dollars a day.

rows.label: Life satisfaction gained per person (food, goods and money branch)
rows.explainer: 0: the food, goods and money are counted at their money value above, and the relief they bring is that value, counted once (the family's wellbeing gain from the same food would be the same change counted twice). Wellbeing is counted in the community and worship branches, where there is no money value.

rows.label: Years the wellbeing effect lasts
rows.explainer: Unused while the gain above is 0: one year, the flow against one year's cost, so nothing would change if a gain were added later.

rows.label: WELLBYs per person reached (food, goods and money branch), discounted
rows.explainer: Point-years, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Illness averted per person reached by food, goods and money, in DALYs
rows.explainer: 0: no study shows a health effect of food-pantry food or one-off bill help in the US beyond what its money value already captures. Health is counted in the rehabilitation branch.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person reached by food, goods and money
rows.explainer: 0: no evidence that the food, goods or bill help averts deaths in the US. Deaths are counted in the shelter and rehabilitation branches.

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted (shelter and recovery) that are of children under five
rows.explainer: 0: the deaths counted are of adults in shelters and in the recovery programme (both serve adults; families in shelter are counted at adult risks, as the Boston cohort was of adults).

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: 0: adult services, as above.

rows.label: Of the adult deaths averted, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: Unsheltered homeless adults in Boston died at a mean age of 53 (SD 11.4; Roncarati et al. 2018, PMC6142967), so by a normal approximation about 40% of the deaths are before 50; people in addiction recovery are younger (ARC residents are mostly 30-55). 45% (30-70%); the rest at GiveWell's 50-74 weight.

rows.label: Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weights by the age band of each death, times your value of a life: the site's one value of a death.

rows.label: Nights of shelter provided, fiscal 2025

source.title: The Salvation Army USA, 2026 National Annual Report: Financial Summary & Statistical Highlights (fiscal year ended 30 September 2025)

rows.explainer: Emergency shelters (287), temporary housing (124) and residences: the residential and institutional services line. The report's 564,511 institutional-care touchpoints are stays in these residences and are counted through these nights, not again. Meals in them are counted in the food row.

rows.label: Share of the shelter nights that are not recovery-centre beds
rows.explainer: The report doesn't say whether recovery residents' nights (about 8,500 beds, up to 3.1 million nights) are inside its nights of shelter. Their stay is valued in the recovery branch, so they are taken out here for the part that may be inside: 85% (70% if all are inside, 100% if none).

rows.label: Person-years of shelter
rows.explainer: Nights over days in a year: the yearly flow of people sheltered at any one time.

rows.label: Value of a night's shelter to the person (US$)
rows.explainer: What the cheapest alternative roof would cost: a room in a rooming house or single-room-occupancy hotel rents for $300-1,200 a month in most US cities, $10-40 a night. Judgment $20; the full cost of running a shelter bed ($40-80) is not its value to the person, who would never pay it.

rows.label: Sheltered people's consumption per person, as a share of the US average
rows.explainer: People in shelters are among the poorest in the country: many live on SSI ($967 a month in 2025, about $11,600 a year or 20% of the mean) or less. 15% (8-30%), below the food-help clients' 30%.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person-year of shelter
rows.explainer: A year's shelter at its value to the person against their own consumption, on the site's one log scale; a year's flow, so no later years.

rows.label: Death rate of unsheltered homeless adults (per person-year)

source.title: Roncarati et al. (2018), Mortality Among Unsheltered Homeless Adults in Boston, Massachusetts, 2000-2009, JAMA Internal Medicine (PMC copy)
source.quote: The crude mortality rate overall was 3713.2 (95% CI, 3110.9-4397.5) deaths per 100 000 person-years.

rows.explainer: Boston, 2000-2009, 445 adults sleeping rough followed for 3,609 person-years; the 95% interval is the range.

rows.label: Death rate unsheltered vs sheltered homeless adults (age-standardised ratio)

source.title: Roncarati et al. (2018), Mortality Among Unsheltered Homeless Adults in Boston, Massachusetts, 2000-2009, JAMA Internal Medicine (PMC copy)
source.quote: the all-cause mortality rate was almost 3-fold larger than that for a cohort of homeless adults primarily sleeping in shelters

rows.explainer: Against Boston's sheltered homeless cohort, same city and decade.

rows.label: Share of the unsheltered-sheltered death gap that shelter itself causes
rows.explainer: People who sleep rough differ from those who use shelters (more untreated mental illness and heavy drinking), so only part of the gap is the roof: exposure, assaults and untreated illness. 30% (10-60%); there is no trial. This is the evidence question for the deaths only, so it sits in the effect, not in shelter_evidence_adj.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person-year of shelter (before the counterfactual)
rows.explainer: The excess death rate of sleeping rough that shelter removes, for a person who would otherwise sleep rough (the counterfactual share is below).

rows.label: People placed in permanent housing, fiscal 2025

source.title: The Salvation Army USA, 2026 National Annual Report: Financial Summary & Statistical Highlights (fiscal year ended 30 September 2025)

rows.explainer: Moves from shelter or the street into permanent or supportive housing (244 permanent and supportive residences, 108 homeless-diversion programmes, veterans' rapid rehousing).

rows.label: Share of placements into permanent supportive housing (rather than rapid re-housing or diversion)
rows.explainer: The report lists 244 permanent and supportive residences against 108 homeless-diversion programmes and 44 veterans' rapid re-housing programmes; diversion and rapid re-housing place many more people per programme than a residence fills. 30% (10-60%).

rows.label: Extra years housed per placement into supportive housing, against usual care
rows.explainer: At Home/Chez Soi, the randomised trial of Housing First (Canada, 2009-2013): participants were stably housed about 73% of the following two years against about 32% in usual care, some 0.8 extra years. The difference between arms is already net of what usual care achieves, so there is no separate counterfactual for it.

rows.label: Extra years housed per rapid re-housing or diversion placement, against usual care
rows.explainer: HUD's Family Options Study (randomised, 2,282 families) found rapid re-housing did little for housing stability against usual care over three years (a few points less time homeless), while long-term subsidies did much more; diversion keeps some people out of shelter for months. 0.15 years (0.05-0.5).

rows.label: Years over which the extra housed time accrues
rows.explainer: The trials' follow-ups: two years for At Home/Chez Soi, three for Family Options. 2 (2-3).

rows.label: Extra years housed per placement (against usual care), discounted
rows.formula: (placement_supportive_share * supportive_years_gained + (1 - placement_supportive_share) * rapid_years_gained) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, placement_followup_years) / placement_followup_years
rows.explainer: The two kinds of placement weighted by their share; each is a trial's difference between arms, so what would have happened anyway is in it. Spread evenly over the follow-up and discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: The Salvation Army's share of the resources behind a placement
rows.explainer: Housing authorities' vouchers, other agencies' rent subsidies and host families pay part of a placed person's housing; the Salvation Army pays the case management, deposits and some rent. Its share, 70% (40-100%): diversion to family is mostly its own work, supportive housing mostly others' subsidies. The rest of the charity's work uses its own resources and volunteers (attribution_share).

rows.label: Share of the extra housed years not already counted as the Salvation Army's own shelter nights
rows.explainer: Some placements are into the Salvation Army's own permanent and supportive residences, whose nights may be inside the report's nights of shelter (the report doesn't define them). Those years are counted there, so the placement branch counts the rest: 80% (50% if all supportive placements are its own residences and inside the count, 100% if none).

rows.label: Value of one's own home over a shelter bed, per night (US$)
rows.explainer: Privacy, safety, storage and a fixed address: what a tenant gains over a shelter bed. A judgment of $5 a night (0-15), a quarter of a room's rent.

rows.label: Rent the placed tenant pays, as a share of their consumption
rows.explainer: Tenants in supportive housing and with vouchers pay 30% of their income; rapid re-housing subsidies taper to zero within months, diversion often moves people in with family. About half pay 30%: 15% (5-25%) of consumption, their own money, taken off the value.

rows.label: Value of a year housed, to the person placed (US$)
rows.formula: shelter_counterfactual_adj * shelter_value_per_night * 365 + own_home_premium_per_night * 365 - tenant_rent_share * consumption_mean * shelter_consumption_share
rows.explainer: Against the person's alternative: a roof for the share who would otherwise sleep rough (the shelter branch's share), the premium of an own home for everyone, less the rent they pay themselves.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per extra year housed
rows.explainer: On the site's one log scale at a homeless person's consumption.

rows.label: Share of a homeless adult's death rate removed by being housed
rows.explainer: Homeless adults die at three to nine times the rate of housed people their age, mostly from overdoses, heart disease and cancer that housing alone changes slowly; Housing First trials found no significant effect on deaths over two years. 20% (5-40%) of the sheltered rate.

rows.label: Death rate of homeless adults using shelters (per person-year)

source.title: Baggett et al. (2013), Mortality Among Homeless Adults in Boston: Shifts in Causes of Death Over a 15-Year Period, JAMA Internal Medicine (PMC copy)
source.quote: 1,302 deaths occurred during 90,450 person-years of observation

rows.explainer: Boston, 2003-2008, 28,033 adults seen by the Health Care for the Homeless Program: 1,302 deaths over 90,450 person-years, a crude rate of 1,439.5 per 100,000.

rows.label: Deaths averted per extra year housed
rows.explainer: The share of the homeless death rate that housing removes.

rows.label: People in substance-abuse and rehabilitation services, fiscal 2025

source.title: The Salvation Army USA, 2026 National Annual Report: Financial Summary & Statistical Highlights (fiscal year ended 30 September 2025)

rows.explainer: Everyone the report counts in its rehabilitation services, most of them in the Adult Rehabilitation Centers' six-month residential work-therapy programme (the national site: 'Each year, we help more than 150,000 adults through our Adult Rehabilitation Centers'). Many leave within weeks: the effect below is per person counted, dropouts included.

rows.label: Extra people in lasting remission per person counted
rows.explainer: No controlled study of the centres. Anchors: the Western Territory admits about 7,500 people a year to its 24 centres and about a third graduate (Caring magazine, 31 October 2014, https://caringmagazine.org/?p=45715), so of ~155,000 people counted nationally perhaps 30-35,000 are admitted and 10-12,000 graduate (about 7% of those counted), and 20-24,000 leave early (about 14%). Among people with alcohol use disorder who sought help, those who got treatment were about 20 percentage points more likely to be in remission three years on than those who didn't, selection included (Moos & Moos 2006, Addiction, doi:10.1111/j.1360-0443.2006.01310.x); reviews of residential treatment rate the evidence moderate, with outcomes better than or no different from other treatment (Reif et al. 2014, Psychiatric Services, doi:10.1176/appi.ps.201300242; de Andrade et al. 2019, Drug and Alcohol Dependence, doi:10.1016/j.drugalcdep.2019.03.031); most people who recover do so without treatment (Tucker et al. 2020, Alcohol Research: Current Reviews, doi:10.35946/arcr.v40.3.02). A 1978 follow-up of a Salvation Army programme found 42-77% abstinent six months after discharge, without a control group (Journal of Studies on Alcohol 39(7):1267-1275). 15 points for graduates (20 less selection) and 3 for those who leave early, over everyone counted: 0.07 × 0.15 + 0.14 × 0.03 = 0.015, range 0.005-0.06.

rows.label: Disability weight of a moderate alcohol use disorder
rows.explainer: The GBD's weight for moderate alcohol use disorder (0.373), shared on the site. Residents with drug dependence carry higher weights (opioid dependence is higher), those with mild disorders lower; the shared fact's range covers it.

rows.label: Years a remission gained lasts, compared with no treatment
rows.explainer: Relapse is common, and many who don't get treatment now remit later, so the gain is years brought forward, not a lifetime: 3 years (1-8), anchored on relapse curves after residential treatment (most relapse in the first year; those abstinent at a year mostly stay so) and natural remission of 5-15% a year.

rows.label: Illness averted per person counted, in DALYs (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Extra remissions × the disability weight lifted × the years they last, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Excess yearly death rate of continued heavy use over remission
rows.explainer: People with alcohol or drug dependence in treatment die at 3-5 times the rate of others their age (about 0.3% a year at 45 in the US), and remission removes much of the gap: about 1% a year (0.5-2%). Anchor: Boston's sheltered homeless adults, many of them dependent, died at 1.4% a year (sheltered_homeless_mortality, Baggett et al. 2013).

rows.label: Deaths averted per person counted (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Extra remissions × the excess death rate they remove × the years, discounted. A harm is left in unmodelled_benefits_adj: people who relapse after a stretch of abstinence face a higher overdose risk.

rows.label: Community centre and Kroc centre participants, fiscal 2025

source.title: The Salvation Army USA, 2026 National Annual Report: Financial Summary & Statistical Highlights (fiscal year ended 30 September 2025)

rows.explainer: Youth clubs, sports, music, after-school programmes and seniors' activities in 1,081 corps community centres and 26 Kroc centres.

rows.label: Summer and day camp participants, fiscal 2025

source.title: The Salvation Army USA, 2026 National Annual Report: Financial Summary & Statistical Highlights (fiscal year ended 30 September 2025)

rows.explainer: Children at the 39 camps and day camps.

rows.label: Senior citizens served, fiscal 2025

source.title: The Salvation Army USA, 2026 National Annual Report: Financial Summary & Statistical Highlights (fiscal year ended 30 September 2025)

rows.explainer: Lunch clubs, activities and visits for older people.

rows.label: People in community, camp and seniors' programmes
rows.explainer: Touchpoints, so some people are counted more than once; the gain below is per person counted and is set low for that reason.

rows.label: Life satisfaction gained per participant while it lasts (points, 0-10)
rows.explainer: Most participants come a few times; regular ones get company, activity and structure. A meta-analysis of interventions for lonely older adults living in the community found group-based programmes reduce loneliness by 0.27 SD (95% CI 0.08-0.48; Shekelle et al. 2024, Journal of General Internal Medicine, doi:10.1007/s11606-023-08517-5); for the regulars that is about 0.2-0.5 life-satisfaction points. Spread over everyone counted, most of them occasional, 0.03 points (0.005-0.1).

rows.label: Years the community programmes' effect lasts
rows.explainer: The effect lasts while people take part: half a year on average (a season to a year).

rows.label: WELLBYs per community participant, discounted
rows.explainer: Point-years, at the shared discount rate.

rows.label: Church members (soldiers and adherents), fiscal 2025

source.title: The Salvation Army USA, 2026 National Annual Report: Financial Summary & Statistical Highlights (fiscal year ended 30 September 2025)

rows.explainer: The Salvation Army is a church: much of the corps line pays for worship, Bible study and fellowship. Members are the people who take part regularly (attendance, 3.7 million, counts visits).

rows.label: Life satisfaction gained by a member from the congregation (points, 0-10)
rows.explainer: Regular churchgoers report higher life satisfaction, mostly through friendships in the congregation (Lim and Putnam 2010, American Sociological Review, about 0.2-0.4 points in US panel data, partly selection). 0.2 (0-0.5) for a year of membership.

rows.label: WELLBYs per member, discounted
rows.explainer: One year's membership, against one year's cost.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, food, goods and money
rows.explainer: 1: the value is priced, not estimated from a study, and its uncertainty is in the prices and in-kind shares above; 0.9 for prices that may not match what was given. How well the counts reflect help delivered is implementation_adj's question alone.

rows.label: Share of the food, goods and money that families wouldn't have got anyway
rows.explainer: No study measures what Salvation Army clients would have got otherwise. Anchors from Feeding America's Hunger in America 2014 (https://www.gbfb.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/08/hunger-in-america-2014-full-report.pdf): 72.7% of food programmes had turned no client away in the past year (p. 79, Table 3-18), so a family not served by the Salvation Army could usually get food at another programme, which argues for a low share; but those programmes' food is itself limited by their donations, so a family served elsewhere takes food another family would have had, and only the part of the Salvation Army's help that other programmes' spare food and family would have covered is not additional. SNAP (54.8% of client households, p. 154) is the families' own baseline and is already in their consumption, not a substitute. The step: about half of the help replaces spare capacity or family help, half is additional: 50% (30-80%).

rows.label: Missing-data discount, food, goods, money and services
rows.explainer: Thin: the counts (meals, items, households helped with bills) are the Salvation Army's own, but the value families get beyond what they would have had anyway is a judgment (the counterfactual, the cash-equivalence of in-kind help, the clients' consumption), with no controlled evaluation of these services. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, shelter
rows.explainer: 1: the value of a bed and the death gap are measured and their uncertainty is in the rows above (the causal share of the death gap is its own row). Down to 0.8 if the Boston gap overstates today's risk of sleeping rough elsewhere. Count quality is implementation_adj's question alone.

rows.label: Share of shelter nights that would otherwise have been spent without a roof
rows.explainer: The same logic as the aid branch: another shelter's bed is a substitute only where beds stand empty. Year-round shelter beds in US cities are mostly full (HUD's Housing Inventory Count puts utilisation of emergency beds near or above 90%), and 36% of people homeless on a January 2024 night were unsheltered (HUD point-in-time count), so a person without a Salvation Army bed mostly takes no one else's bed: they sleep rough, or double up with family or friends (a roof, but often unstable). The step: about a tenth find a spare shelter bed and about two-fifths double up, half sleep rough: 50% (30-70%). The value and the deaths both count only for them; the placements' alternative reads the same share.

rows.label: Missing-data discount, shelter
rows.explainer: Thin: nights are counted, but the deaths a bed averts come from Boston cohorts of other shelters' clients and what a night replaces is a judgment; there is no evaluation of these shelters. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, housing placements
rows.explainer: The years housed are anchored on a trial of a better-supported programme; 0.8 for placements counted at move-in whatever happens next.

rows.label: Share of the placements' gain other agencies wouldn't have provided beyond usual care
rows.explainer: 1: the years housed are trial differences against usual care, which already includes other agencies and leaving homelessness without help. Down to 0.8 where other programmes would have placed the same people with more support than the trials' usual care.

rows.label: Missing-data discount, housing placements
rows.explainer: Thin: placements are counted, but the years housed they add come from trials of other programmes (a Housing First trial, the Family Options Study), not of these placements. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, recovery programme
rows.explainer: The remission gain is a judgment without a controlled study of these centres: 0.6 for reported outcomes of faith-based residential programmes running above controlled results, and for selection (people who stay are those likeliest to recover anyway).

rows.label: Share of residents who wouldn't have had other treatment
rows.explainer: The centres take people with no insurance and no money, but some would have found a public or Medicaid-funded programme. 70% (40-90%); the remission gain is against no treatment.

rows.label: Missing-data discount, recovery programme
rows.explainer: Thin: residents are counted, but the remission gain is a judgment anchored on the residential-treatment literature; the centres have no controlled evaluation. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, community programmes
rows.explainer: The gain is anchored on trials of more intensive programmes than drop-in activities: 0.6.

rows.label: Share of community participation that wouldn't have happened elsewhere
rows.explainer: YMCAs, Boys & Girls Clubs, public parks and senior centres offer much the same in most towns: half.

rows.label: Missing-data discount, community programmes
rows.explainer: Thin: participants are counted, but the life-satisfaction gain is a judgment anchored on trials of more intensive programmes. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, worship
rows.explainer: The association of churchgoing with life satisfaction is partly selection; panel studies halve it: 0.5.

rows.label: Share of members who wouldn't be in another congregation
rows.explainer: Most members of a Salvation Army corps would belong to another church without it: 15% (5-40%).

rows.label: Missing-data discount, worship
rows.explainer: Thin: members are counted, but the life-satisfaction gain is a judgment from observational studies of churchgoing. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment: outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row (aid_evidence_adj, shelter_evidence_adj, placement_evidence_adj, rehab_evidence_adj, community_evidence_adj, worship_evidence_adj), weighted by its outcome before adjustments in healthy years (each branch through its unit's fixed bridge).
rows.formula: (aid_dalys_unadjusted * aid_evidence_adj + shelter_dalys_unadjusted * shelter_evidence_adj + placement_dalys_unadjusted * placement_evidence_adj + rehab_dalys_unadjusted * rehab_evidence_adj + community_dalys_unadjusted * community_evidence_adj + worship_dalys_unadjusted * worship_evidence_adj) / (aid_dalys_unadjusted + shelter_dalys_unadjusted + placement_dalys_unadjusted + rehab_dalys_unadjusted + community_dalys_unadjusted + worship_dalys_unadjusted)

rows.label: Counterfactual: outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row (aid_counterfactual_adj, shelter_counterfactual_adj, placement_counterfactual_adj, rehab_counterfactual_adj, community_counterfactual_adj, worship_counterfactual_adj), weighted by its outcome before adjustments in healthy years (each branch through its unit's fixed bridge).
rows.formula: (aid_dalys_unadjusted * aid_counterfactual_adj + shelter_dalys_unadjusted * shelter_counterfactual_adj + placement_dalys_unadjusted * placement_counterfactual_adj + rehab_dalys_unadjusted * rehab_counterfactual_adj + community_dalys_unadjusted * community_counterfactual_adj + worship_dalys_unadjusted * worship_counterfactual_adj) / (aid_dalys_unadjusted + shelter_dalys_unadjusted + placement_dalys_unadjusted + rehab_dalys_unadjusted + community_dalys_unadjusted + worship_dalys_unadjusted)

rows.label: Volunteers, fiscal 2025

source.title: The Salvation Army USA, 2026 National Annual Report: Financial Summary & Statistical Highlights (fiscal year ended 30 September 2025)

rows.explainer: Most ring bells at the red kettles at Christmas or sort and hand out food and toys.

rows.label: Hours given per volunteer in the year
rows.explainer: No published total. Most are kettle bell-ringers doing one or a few two-hour shifts; a minority volunteer weekly. 8 hours (3-20).

rows.label: Value of a volunteer hour, United States, 2025

source.title: Independent Sector and Do Good Institute, Value of Volunteer Time (2025)
source.quote: the estimate for the value of a volunteer hour was $36.14 in 2025

rows.explainer: Average private-sector earnings excluding farm and managerial work: the local wage Convention 2 asks for.

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: The Salvation Army's spending already includes the government grants ($540M) and donated goods it uses, so only its volunteers' unpaid hours, at the US volunteer wage, are resources from outside its cost. Partner food banks' food arrives as recorded in-kind gifts and is in the cost.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (fidelity, compliance, follow-through)
rows.explainer: The one row for count quality. Every count here is the charity's own administrative tally (touchpoints, meals converted from pounds of pantry food, nights held rather than slept), with no independent check; some double counting across units is likely. Cross-check of the largest count: the Western Territory recorded $109.3M of donated food and $5.7M of government food in fiscal 2023 (statements, note 7); scaled to the nation by its share of the households helped (wt_share_of_households, 24%), that is about $480M of food, or about 178M meals at the Thrifty Food Plan's $2.70 a meal, against 184M meals reported; donated food is valued below retail, so the food would make somewhat more meals, and some of it feeds shelter and centre residents counted as nights. The meal count holds up; the other counts are touchpoints with no such check. 90% (70-100%) for every branch.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: 1: government grants are tied to contracts the Salvation Army delivers; a donation doesn't free government money for other uses or pull in much more. 0.9 if some local governments fund less where the Salvation Army is present.

rows.label: Net assets available for operations, 30 September 2025

source.title: The Salvation Army USA, 2026 National Annual Report: Unaudited Combined Statement of Financial Position

rows.explainer: Unrestricted money not designated for buildings or specific programmes: what a new gift joins before it is spent. Endowments and designated funds are left out, since a new gift doesn't wait behind them.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value

They roughly cancel: 0 (-10% to +15%). The 7.3 million personal connections (intake interviews, case management, information requests, p. 21) are how the counted help is delivered, not help of their own.
